mcqs.question: How does requiring a quorum (a strict majority) prevent split-brain during a network partition?
options: A partition can produce at most one side with a majority of the cluster, so the minority side must refuse to act as leader or accept writes
It guarantees the partition heals within a fixed time window
It doubles the number of nodes automatically to compensate for the partition
It requires every node to agree on a value before any read is allowed
mcqs.explanation: Quorum works because a majority is mathematically impossible on two sides of the same split at once — at most one side can have more than half the nodes, so the other side is forced to refuse action. It doesn't affect how fast a partition heals, doesn't add nodes, and this specific mechanism concerns writes/leadership, not read unanimity.

mcqs.question: What should happen if a partition splits the cluster such that neither side reaches quorum?
options: One side should be chosen at random to continue accepting writes
Both sides should continue accepting writes and reconcile the conflicts later
Neither side should accept writes — the system deliberately becomes unavailable for writes until connectivity is restored
The cluster should automatically remove nodes until one side has a majority
mcqs.explanation: Refusing writes on both sides is the correct, deliberate CP choice: it avoids the divergence that would come from letting either side act without a majority. Random selection or letting both sides proceed reintroduces exactly the split-brain risk; auto-removing nodes during a partition you can't fully observe is unsafe.

mcqs.question: How do fencing tokens complement quorum in preventing split-brain damage?
options: Fencing tokens replace the need for quorum entirely
Fencing tokens only matter for read operations, never writes
Fencing tokens make quorum checks unnecessary once a leader is elected
Quorum prevents two leaders from being elected simultaneously; fencing tokens are a second layer that rejects a stale write even if an old leader briefly still believes it's in charge
mcqs.explanation: The two mechanisms cover different moments: quorum governs who can become or remain leader, while fencing governs what happens if a stale leader still tries to write despite having lost that status. Neither replaces the other, and fencing specifically matters for writes, not just reads.

mcqs.question: Why is using an even number of nodes for a quorum group a weaker choice than an odd number?
options: Even-sized clusters cannot use the majority-vote formula at all
An even split can leave neither side with a strict majority, losing write availability more easily than an odd-sized cluster achieving the same fault tolerance would
Even numbers of nodes are more expensive to run in the cloud
Even-sized clusters always elect the wrong leader
mcqs.explanation: An even-sized cluster can split into two equal halves, neither reaching a strict majority — a safe but availability-losing outcome that an odd-sized cluster (which cannot split evenly) avoids for the same number of tolerated failures. The majority formula still applies to even clusters; this isn't about cost or leader-election correctness.
